title: What does one merge cost?
hook: Two sorted piles must become one sorted row. How many comparisons can that cost?
misconception: Splitting a problem into pieces adds work; merging is cleanup at the end.
objective: The learner can explain why merging two sorted piles of total size n needs at most n-1 comparisons, and why that makes splitting worthwhile.

claims.text: Merging two sorted lists with n elements in total takes at most n-1 comparisons.
claims.source: Each comparison outputs one element; the last element needs no comparison. Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 5.2.4.

claims.text: Merge Sort sorts 1,000 items in fewer than 10,000 comparisons in the worst case.
claims.source: Worst case n*ceil(log2 n) - 2^ceil(log2 n) + 1 = 1000*10 - 1024 + 1 = 8,977 (Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 5.2.4).

claims.text: Comparing every one of 1,000 cards with every other takes 499,500 comparisons.
Merging two sorted piles of 4 cards can need as many as 7 comparisons, so 7 is the most you could ever need.
claims.source: Upper bound from c1 (n-1 = 7). Tightness: interleaved piles (A holds the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th smallest; B the rest) force a comparison for each of the first 7 cards. Brute force over all 70 splits of 8 distinct values gives max 7. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-12 from the predict answer and reveal; needs an independent check.

claims.text: Once one pile is empty, the remaining cards go into the row with no further comparisons.
claims.source: The remaining pile is already sorted and every card in it is larger than everything placed so far, so it is appended as is. Seen in the reveal ("the rest just slides over for free") and the stage message "One pile is empty. The rest needs no comparisons." Added by fact-checker 2026-10-12; needs an independent check.

claims.text: Two sorted piles holding 10 cards in total need at most 9 comparisons to merge, and some piles need all 9.
claims.source: c1 with n = 10 gives at most 9; brute force over every split (1+9 up to 5+5) reaches 9. Recall question answer and its why ("Every comparison places one card for good, and the last card needs none"). Added by fact-checker 2026-10-12; needs an independent check.

claims.text: Splitting the cards into piles costs no comparisons; all of Merge Sort's comparisons happen while merging.
claims.source: Top-down Merge Sort splits by position (first half / second half) without looking at values, so the split step makes zero comparisons; the comparison count W(n) = W(ceil(n/2)) + W(floor(n/2)) + (merge cost) has no split term. Hook ("looks like extra work. It isn't.") and reveal ("The splitting is setup."). Added by fact-checker 2026-10-12; needs an independent check. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: VERIFIED by a different checker session from the 2026-10-12 author: own instrumented top-down merge sort over all 40,320 orders of 8 cards counts comparisons only in the merge loop; split is by slicing.

claims.text: Halving 1,000 cards down to single cards takes 10 rounds, and each round of merges costs fewer than 1,000 comparisons (it places every card once), so Merge Sort needs fewer than 10,000 comparisons, while checking every pair would take 499,500.
claims.source: Top-down Merge Sort: recursion depth ceil(log2 1000) = 10. At each depth the merges together place at most n cards, each merge of k cards costs at most k-1 (c1), so a level costs fewer than n = 1000. 10 levels give fewer than 10,000; exact worst case 8,977 (c2). Reveal paragraph 2 (v2). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node (fc22-5/ms.mjs): top-down recursion depth for 1,000 is 10 = ceil(log2 1000); worst case 8,977 < 10,000; 1000 x 999 / 2 = 499,500. Per-level cards placed: 1,000 at each of the first 9 levels and 976 at the 10th, so 'places every card once' is exact for 9 of 10 rounds and 'at most once' for the last; the bound (fewer comparisons than cards per round) holds either way. Non-blocking wording nit for the builder: 'places each card at most once'. | REVISED v5 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): reveal reworded: 'Halving 1,000 cards takes 10 rounds, each under 1,000 comparisons: fewer than 10,000, against 499,500 for every pair.'. Unverified.

claims.text: Checking every pair of 8 cards takes 28 comparisons.
claims.source: C(8,2) = 8*7/2 = 28. Reveal paragraph 2 (v2), linking the predict distractor 28 to the 499,500 of c3.

claims.text: Merge Sort on 8 cards needs at most 4 + 6 + 7 = 17 comparisons (four merges of 1+1 cards cost 1 each, two merges of 2+2 cost at most 3 each, one merge of 4+4 costs at most 7), against 28 for checking every pair.
claims.source: Merging two sorted lists with n cards in total takes at most n-1 comparisons (claim c1); 4*1 + 2*3 + 7 = 17; C(8,2) = 28. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: brute force over all 40,320 orders of 8 cards, worst case 17 comparisons; C(8,2) = 28.

claims.text: On the stage the deck the piles came from is shown in three stacked rounds: split into 8 single cards (0 comparisons), merge singles into pairs (4), merge pairs into piles A and B (6). With the final merge's count added (7 for the first piles), the whole sort costs 0 + 4 + 6 + 7 = 17, against 28 for every pair.
claims.source: deal() in Demo.tsx computes the rounds with the same two-pointer merge the learner does. The deck order [l2, l0, l3, l1, r3, r1, r0, r2] is fixed, so every pair needs its 1 comparison (4) and each 2+2 merge interleaves to the end (3 + 3 = 6) for every seed; checked in node for seeds 7, 20, 33, 46. Seed 7 piles A 10 20 21 23 and B 4 5 18 36 interleave to the end, so the final merge is 7. 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 pairs (claim c10). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node port of deal(): pairCost 4 and fourCost 6 for all 200 seeds 7, 20, 33, ... (seed + 13 steps, as 'New piles' does); seed 7 piles A 10 20 21 23, B 4 5 18 36, final merge 7, so 0 + 4 + 6 + 7 = 17 against 28. RoundsStack draws three rows with those labels; roundLabel shows 'Whole sort: 0 + 4 + 6 + 7 = 17, against 28 for every pair.' | REVISED v5 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): v5: when the merge completes, the rounds' costs and the merge count are recorded and shown in a line 'Your sort: 0 + 4 + 6 + 7 = 17, against 28.' that New piles does not clear; the reveal quotes this record ('The rounds before the last merge cost 4 and 6; with the last merge's 7, the whole sort took 17'). Unverified.

recall.question: Two sorted piles hold 10 cards in total. What is the most comparisons a merge needs?
recall.why: Every comparison places one card for good, and the last card needs none.
